descripcion: At C2 understatement is used with awareness of exactly how much distance it creates from sincerity, and controlled enough to be dropped instantly when a moment calls for directness instead — the mark of command here is knowing when not to use the device, not just how to produce it.

cuadroReferencia.titulo: Knowing when to drop the device
filas: understatement can read as evasive or cold
drop the device the moment sincerity is actually needed

ejemplos.texto: Not the smoothest presentation I've ever given, if I'm honest.
This is serious, and I want to say that plainly, without any of the usual understatement.
I'm not going to make light of this one.

notas: Explicitly naming the switch (without any of the usual understatement) signals to the listener that the register has changed on purpose, which prevents the shift from reading as a mood swing.
A speaker who understates everything, including genuinely serious moments, reads as emotionally unavailable rather than witty.
This is serious, and I want to say that plainly is itself a marked, deliberate move — stating directness explicitly, rather than assuming it will register on its own.

contraste.es: Spanish knows understatement (no está mal, no es precisamente…), so the device is familiar. The C2 skill is knowing when to drop it: in serious or high-stakes moments English switches to plain directness, and understatement there reads as evasive.
contraste.de: German understatement (nicht schlecht, nicht gerade…) works much like English, so the device is familiar. A trap is British quite: quite good often means only fairly good, not ziemlich gut.
contraste.it: Italian litotes (non male, non proprio…) corresponds well to English understatement, so the device is familiar. The C2 skill is knowing when to drop it for plain directness.
contraste.fr: French litotes is familiar, but pas mal can be strongly positive in French (c'est pas mal du tout), while English not bad is milder. French speakers need to recalibrate how strong English understatement is.
contraste.pt: Portuguese nada mau and não é propriamente… correspond well to English understatement, so the device is familiar. The C2 skill is knowing when to drop it for plain directness.

errores: Understating a genuinely serious or painful moment, which can read as cold or evasive.
Switching to directness without any signal, so the shift feels like a change of mood rather than a deliberate register choice.
Overusing the explicit switch-flagging move until it becomes its own tic.

autochequeo: Is understatement avoided in genuinely serious or painful moments?
Is any switch to directness clearly signalled, not just assumed?
Would the listener register the shift as deliberate, not a mood change?
Is the explicit-switch move used sparingly, not as a tic?
Does the overall tone match the actual stakes of the situation?
